t: Okay, here's a headline that stopped me cold this week: models are getting dumber on purpose. Not a bug. On purpose. Apparently the labs are trading away world knowledge for raw reasoning skill.

Right, and the numbers back it up. On math and code benchmarks, models are getting smarter per parameter at an absurd rate. GLM-5.2 scores ninety-nine percent on AIME with about forty billion active parameters. Qwen3.5 does ninety-one percent with seventeen billion active.
Which is wild when you remember GPT-4 in 2023 supposedly ran around two hundred eighty billion active parameters, and it could barely solve an AIME problem.
But then you ask these same razor-sharp models a plain factual question, no tools allowed, and the picture completely flips.
Yeah, there's this benchmark called SimpleQA, pure factual recall. The current leader is Gemini 2.5 Pro at fifty-three percent. So the best recall money can buy still misses half the questions!

And the small models barely register. Qwen3.5 four and nine billion parameter models have hallucination rates of eighty to eighty-two percent on knowledge tests. Meaning when they don't know a fact, which is most of the time, they just make one up.
So you get this confident, plausible, completely wrong answer if you ask for, say, the birth year of some minor nineteenth-century mathematician.
Exactly. And the key point is: the parameter count didn't drop for free. This is a deliberate trade. Labs are trading world knowledge for reasoning skill.
Okay, so why would that trade make sense? I feel like knowledge is kind of the whole point of an AI.

Well, facts take space. Literally. There's this research series, Physics of Language Models, with the cleanest measurements, and it puts knowledge capacity at roughly two bits of factual knowledge per parameter.

Two bits per parameter... so if you want a model that knows the birth year of every minor Wikipedia figure, the population of every Dutch municipality, and the argument order of every npm function ever—
—you pay for that in weights. And that's a big part of why frontier models grew to trillions of parameters.

Whereas reasoning compresses much better, because it's really just a small set of procedures applied over and over. Break the problem down, track your state, check your work, backtrack when something fails.

And it turns out distillation and reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks transfer those procedures into small models remarkably well. There's this model, Phi-4, fourteen billion parameters, trained heavily on synthetic textbook-style data. Great at math, terrible at trivia. Which tells you exactly what was in its training data.
And here's the kicker, that used to look like a limitation of synthetic data. Now it looks like the design goal.
There's a second reason the trade makes sense, and honestly I think it's the strongest one: facts rot, procedures don't.
Meaning a frontier training run takes months, costs hundreds of millions of dollars, and the moment it finishes, the facts inside start going stale.
Library APIs change, prices change, people change jobs. Half of what a 2024 model believed about the JavaScript ecosystem was outdated before the model even shipped.
But algebra worked the same in 1970 as it does now. Same with decomposing a problem or spotting a contradiction between two sources. Procedures don't age.

So a model that's mostly procedure, only lightly loaded with facts, doesn't age the way a knowledge-heavy model does. Its training cutoff matters way less, because current events were never supposed to live in the weights in the first place.

And notice what knowledge does survive has a particular shape. These models are generalists. They know a little about nearly everything, almost nothing in depth. Ask about PostgreSQL, they know what it is and roughly how it works. Ask which version added a specific planner feature—invented facts.

But that's actually the right layer to keep. Breadth is what lets the model understand the question, know what to look up, and judge whether a source is plausible. Depth is cheap to retrieve and expensive to store, so depth is what goes.
Okay, so if the model doesn't know things, something else has to. And that something is the harness, right? Retrieval, tool calls, web search, a filesystem full of docs.

The model contributes the reasoning, everything it reasons about gets supplied at runtime. And honestly, coding agents already work this way. The agent doesn't memorize your dependency's API surface. It greps node_modules or reads the docs before calling anything.

Which means its answer is grounded in the version you actually have installed, not whichever version dominated the training data. The recall that used to be a fixed cost in every forward pass becomes an on-demand lookup.
Now follow the trend out a couple of years, and here's where it gets spicy. The author's prediction: frontier-quality reasoning, Fable-quality, running on a single consumer GPU.
How? The compute half is nearly there already. DeepSeek V4-Flash reasons with about thirteen billion active parameters per token. Totally consumer-GPU territory.

What doesn't fit is the other two hundred seventy-one billion parameters sitting in its expert layers. But expert layers are mostly fact storage. That's exactly the part this trade makes optional. Strip the knowledge out, and total size shrinks toward active size. A twenty to forty billion parameter model at four-bit quantization fits on a twenty-four gig card from 2022.
No per-token bill, no data leaving the machine. The catch, of course: it won't know much. Ask it a bare factual question and the correct behavior is to say, I don't know, let me look it up.

Which brings us to maybe my favorite part, the hallucination argument. When a fact lives in weights, a wrong fact is unfindable and unfixable. You can't grep the weights. You can't diff them against last month. Fixing one error means a fine-tune that might break who knows what else.

But when the fact lives outside the model, a wrong answer has an address. The model cites a document, you can open the document. If the document is wrong, you fix the document, and every future query gets the correction.
Which beats waiting for the next training run by roughly a year.
It's not zero hallucination, the model can still misread a source or stitch two of them together wrong. But a claim with a source is checkable. A claim from weights isn't.
A wrong fact in a knowledge base just becomes an ordinary data bug. The kind engineers already know how to trace, fix, and write a regression test for.

So the provocative reframe here is that hallucination was never really a bug to train away. It's an architecture smell. Keep facts in weights and wrongness is invisible. Move the facts out and it becomes a manageable data problem.

There's even a version of this future where the model card stops listing a knowledge cutoff at all, because what's left in the weights goes stale on a scale of years, not weeks. The model just gets handed the world's current state at runtime—
—the same way a CPU gets handed a program.
So, dumber on purpose turns out to be: smarter where it counts, cheaper where it matters, and more honest about what it doesn't know. Not a bad trade.
Dumber is the new smarter. Alright, that's the show. Links in the notes, and we'll catch you next time!
